- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.

message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to buy the Pacific Avenue property or start an auction.

I have $505 and own one of three greens. Buying Pacific Avenue for $300 would give me two greens and leave $205. I still need to decide if this is worth the cash.

I should keep cash liquid for face denial. Two greens would block p2 from a green monopoly, but $205 is too tight to cover Marvin at $280. I will not fuel opponents.

Auctioning Pacific Avenue could let p2 acquire it cheaply. They would still need my North Carolina to complete a green monopoly, so they would bid aggressively. p1 has no greens and no cash to spend.

p3 has $800 and no greens, so they might bid. If I auction Pacific, p2 could acquire it cheaply or pay a premium. Buying it myself would make me the green gatekeeper with two of three properties. That would be stronger than letting p2 hold two greens while I keep only one.

I can still afford Tennessee at face value for $180, leaving $25. A railroad at $200 would leave only $5. Marvin is out of reach at $280. No monopolies exist yet, so rent risk is low. p1 needs Tennessee to complete oranges, and my Connecticut blocks the light blues.

p2 holds one red, one green, one pink, and Boardwalk. p3 holds Baltic, Electric, Virginia, Atlantic, and Park Place. No monopolies exist yet. Buying Pacific at face value is the correct denial play.
